Serjeant
SAR-junt
noun
From the Latin serviens, “one serving,” through the Old French sergent; hence an officer who serves a court or magistrate. In the KJV it renders the Roman lictor — the attendant who bore the fasces and executed the magistrate’s sentence.

Biblical Definition

A serjeant in the KJV is a Roman lictor — the officer who attended a magistrate, bore before him the bundled rods and axe of his authority, and carried out his commands of arrest, scourging, and release. It is not the sergeant of a modern army. The word belongs to the story of Philippi, where Paul and Silas were beaten and jailed without trial. When the magistrates, alarmed at the earthquake and the jailer’s report, wished to be rid of their prisoners quietly, “the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go” (Act 16:35). But Paul would not slink out by a side door: they had beaten Romans openly and uncondemned, and should fetch them openly. “And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans” (Act 16:38). The same officers who had earlier stood by as “the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them” (Act 16:22) now came trembling to escort them out. The serjeant is the visible edge of the magistrate’s power, the hand that holds the rod — and Scripture teaches that this power, rightly used, is God’s own ordinance: “he is the minister of God to thee for good… for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). The lictor’s rods at Philippi were wielded unjustly against innocent men, and the magistrates learned to fear; but the office itself, the bearing of the sword under authority, is appointed of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

An officer who serves a court or magistrate; in the KJV, a Roman lictor, bearer of the rods of office.

SERJEANT, an officer who attends a magistrate or court to execute its commands.

From Latin serviens, “one serving,” through Old French sergent.

In the KJV it renders the Roman lictor, who bore the fasces of office.

The magistrates of Philippi sent the serjeants to release Paul and Silas (Act 16:35).

The serjeants brought back word, and the magistrates feared (Act 16:38).

Key Scripture

Act 16:35 — "And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go."

Act 16:38 — "And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans."

Act 16:22 — "And the multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them."

Rom 13:4 — "For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Modern Corruption

Not a military sergeant but a Roman lictor, the magistrate’s officer; the word recovers the lawful bearing of the sword under authority.

expand to see more

The honest confusion here is with the modern soldier. We hear “serjeant” and think of the drill-sergeant, the non-commissioned officer of an army; but the KJV means the lictor, the civil officer who walked before a Roman magistrate bearing the fasces — the bound rods and axe that were the very emblem of the power to scourge and to execute. At Philippi the serjeants were the hands that carried out the magistrates’ unjust sentence, and then the hands sent trembling to undo it. To read the word rightly is to see the machinery of Roman justice up close: the magistrate who commands, and the officer at his side who bears the rod and does the deed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sword borne under authority. The lictor’s rods are the very thing Paul has in view when he writes that the ruler beareth not the sword in vain, for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. God has committed to the civil power a real and dreadful instrument, and the serjeant is that instrument in a man’s hand. At Philippi it was drawn against the innocent, and the magistrates were made to fear when they learned whom they had beaten; the abuse of the sword brings its own reckoning. Yet the office is holy, and the Christian neither despises it as the anarchist does nor worships it as the tyrant’s flatterer does. He honours the sword as God’s ordinance and trembles that it is not borne in vain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means an officer serving a magistrate; in the KJV, a Roman lictor who bore the rods of office.

Serjeant — Latin serviens, “one serving,” via Old French sergent.

It renders the Roman lictor, attendant of the magistrate.

Not a military sergeant, but a civil officer bearing the fasces.

The serjeants were sent to release Paul from the Philippian jail (Act 16:35).

They feared when they learned they had beaten Romans (Act 16:38).

Usage

"A serjeant in the KJV is a lictor, not an army sergeant: the magistrate’s officer with the rods."

"The magistrates sent the serjeants to let them go — but Paul demanded an open release."

"The serjeant bears the rod: he beareth not the sword in vain, for he is God’s minister."
